line:
I step onto the quay, wring out my cloak, and meet the arbiter's eyes. "Madam, three of the Heron's Tithe's hands lie dead in our skiff, killed when they attacked us at the Gullspit light, and their master is a hooded man called Aldous, who sailed off with a man named Sparrow. May I give you the full account, and read Corvin's statement, indoors and by a fire?"

DM: also, is there any word yet on whether Corvin has signed his statement and named the man he called "H."?

entries.text: dice Wren's Persuasion getting the arbiter to hear her indoors and share Corvin's statement (exhaustion 1 disadvantage), DC 12: 1d20+5 (disadvantage) = 1d20 [3, 18]→3 + 5 = 8

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~10:30 AM: per the arbiter, Corvin signed a statement overnight, but it names no 'H.' and says only that Elowen was last seen at Ashby Weir and that a 'grey-sailed patron' paid him for years to watch for her heir. The arbiter holds it sealed; she will let Wren read it only after Wren's account is taken and the dead hands are examined. Corvin asks again to see Wren.

entries.text:
Your Persuasion check was an 8 with disadvantage. It isn't enough to charm the arbiter, but it doesn't have to be. She is a practical woman and the dead men are plain evidence.

She looks at the three covered shapes, then at the lamp still burning white across the water. "Indoors, then," she says. "Pell, have the dead taken to the hall's cold room and counted. Mistress Ashgrove, you will have a fire. You will not have the statement until your account is down, because I do not hand a witness another witness's words before she has given her own."

In the Vantry hall's counting-room, with a fire, a blanket and hot cider, you give the whole account: the Wick-House, the staff, Sparrow, the cutter, the three hands, the grey-cloaked man called Aldous. Kit adds her dry corrections. The arbiter's stylus never stops. When you finish, she sets it down.

On your question she is plain. "He signed in the night. It names no 'H.' He says only that Elowen was last seen at Ashby Weir, and that for years a grey-sailed patron paid him to watch for her heir." She raises an eyebrow. "He says it was a patron, not a master. I'd say that is a distinction without a difference, but he insists. I hold it sealed. You may read it when I have counted your dead and sent to the keep. Tomorrow morning." She pauses. "He asks for you again. He says he has the rest, and he'll give it to you alone."

It is half past ten. You have no slots, and you are soaked and tired. The lamp is lit, and the town is talking about it.

What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~10:30 AM: his signed statement, taken down by the cellar clerk, was read to Wren in the Vantry hall. It names Elowen's last known places (Ashby Weir, then upriver and downriver), says he sold her blessings, and names the man 'H.' as Hale only as 'a hand of the man I owe', refusing a surname. He signed it at dawn. He did not mention the Gullspit light or 'Aldous'. He asked, through the guard, whether the lamp burning across the estuary was 'hers'.

entries.text:
Your Persuasion check was a 15, even with disadvantage, and it's plenty. The arbiter looks at the three shrouded shapes, then at the white thread of light still burning across the estuary, and her stern face loosens a little. "Pell, take the dead to the hall's cold room and have the dead men's names asked on the quay. Mistress Ashgrove, with me."

In the hall there's a fire, dry blankets and hot spiced cider. Kit gets a stool beside the hearth and doesn't move from it. You give your account in order, and the arbiter's clerk writes it down. You tell her about the hooded man Aldous, Sparrow, the Heron's Tithe, the three hands who attacked at the door, and what Elowen's grave told you. She listens without interrupting, and when you finish she says only, "A grey-sailed cutter has no right to be in my harbour without a Vantry mark. I'll have the harbour-master ask who let her moor."

Then she answers your other question. Corvin's statement is signed. He put his name to it at dawn, and the cellar clerk's hand is neat. She reads you the relevant parts. It names the places he last knew Elowen to be: Ashby Weir, then upriver and downriver. He admits he sold her blessings. As for "H.", he names him only as "a hand of the man I owe", and he refused a surname. It doesn't mention the Gullspit light or anyone called Aldous. "He asked one thing," the arbiter adds, "through the guard. Whether the lamp burning across the estuary was hers."

It's half past ten. You are warm and fed for the first time in hours, but you have no spell slots, and you have a signed statement, three dead men, and a man in the cellar who seems to have stopped lying about at least one thing.

What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~10:15 AM: his written statement is signed (per arbiter). It names 'H.' as 'Hale's elder brother, a river-factor called Hollis Hale', and says only that Elowen's master, a man he calls 'the Lamp-Warden', paid Corvin twenty years ago to find her. The statement does not name Aldous. Arbiter holds it sealed for Dame Crowe, but will let Wren read a copy.

entries.text:
The arbiter takes it in at a glance: the dead men, the wet girl, the lamp burning white through the rain. Your Persuasion was a 7 with disadvantage, but you hardly needed it. "Not on the quay," she says. "Inside. Pell, carry them to the hall and have the physician look at them." She turns and walks.

In the hall's side room there's a fire, and you give your full account, steaming, with Kit adding a dry word where it counts. The arbiter writes without comment until you reach the name. "Aldous," she repeats. "Not a name I know on this coast. I'll have the harbour-reeve ask after a grey-sailed cutter called the Heron's Tithe."

Now your out-of-story question: yes, there is word. Corvin signed his statement last night. The arbiter says it names the "H." he spoke of: Hollis Hale, an elder brother of the Hale now held for Dame Crowe, a river-factor who trades up and down the Marrow. Corvin also says he was paid twenty years ago by a man he calls only "the Lamp-Warden" to find Elowen. He does not name Aldous, and the arbiter notes that this may mean he doesn't know the name or won't give it. She will let you read a copy.

It's a little after ten. You've no spell slots and your reliquary is at the light. What does Wren do?

Your Persuasion check was an 11 with disadvantage, enough against an easy DC. The arbiter looks at the three covered shapes, the rain running off your cloak, and Kit swaying beside you, and nods once. "Indoors. Fire. Pell, take the dead to the hall's cold-room and fetch a physician's boy for the Thistlewood woman." Kit bristles at that and then, quietly, accepts it.

On your out-of-story question: yes. Corvin signed his statement at dusk yesterday. It names the towns and dates of your mother's last years: Ashby Weir, Lantern's Rest, the Wick-House. The "H." he spoke of turns out to be Hale's master-of-hand, not Hale himself, but he gave no further name. The arbiter reads you that much from the sealed copy, and says he told the clerk the rest was "for Wren's ears alone." She holds the full statement under seal for Dame Crowe.

The arbiter writes it all down without comment. When you finish she says, "That makes two of Corvin's ledger's shadows in my town in two days. I'll send a rider to Dame Crowe." She also tells you Corvin is still in the cellar, and asks for you by name every hour.

It's past half past ten. You're wet, tired, and out of spells. A long rest would restore them, and the cellar door is a staircase away. What does Wren do?

Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
